papers.abstract: Baseflow constitutes over half of streamflow in mountainous headwaters of the western United States (US), making accurate quantification critical for water resource management. However, traditional baseflow separation methods are often arbitrary and ambiguous, complicating validation. Here, we developed an integrated hydrologic model coupling surface and subsurface flow to quantify baseflow in the Coal Creek watershed, a snow‐dominated catchment in Colorado, US. A model‐agnostic approach was implemented to estimate baseflow from simulated hydrologic exchange fluxes and these estimates were used as a reference to evaluate four common baseflow separation methods: the Pettyjohn and Henning (PH) graphical, United Kingdom Institute of Hydrology (UKIH) graphical, Eckhardt digital filter, and conductance mass balance (CMB) methods. Both the UKIH and Eckhardt methods performed relatively well, with modified Kling‐Gupta Efficiency values of 0.73 and 0.68 and Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency values of 0.59 and 0.71, respectively. However, the UKIH method underperformed during average and dry years, when stream hydrographs exhibit unimodal peaks typical of snow‐dominated catchments. The PH and CMB methods showed poor performance overall: the PH method substantially overestimated baseflow (average baseflow index (BFI) of 85%) owing to its short moving window, while the CMB method underestimated it (average BFI of 38%), potentially due to the exclusion of interflow contributions, compared to a numerically derived BFI of 58%. These findings highlight the utility of integrated hydrologic models as a reference for evaluating baseflow separation methods, particularly in snow‐dominated catchments where graphical and tracer‐based approaches may misrepresent baseflow contributions.

papers.title: Contrasting Groundwater Response to Surface Water Shortages in the Upper and Lower Colorado River Basins
papers.snippet: Groundwater plays a critical role in sustaining the water supply in the Colorado River Basin (CRB), a region experiencing persistent drought, population growth, and increasing water demand.
papers.abstract: Groundwater plays a critical role in sustaining the water supply in the Colorado River Basin (CRB), a region experiencing persistent drought, population growth, and increasing water demand. Using GRACE/GRACE‐FO satellite observations combined with hydrological data sets, we analyze basin‐scale variations and long‐term trends in terrestrial and groundwater storage across the CRB from water year 2004–2023. We further apply a joint framework integrating copula‐based statistical modeling with statistical inference to quantify probabilistic relationships among storage‐based drought indicators and to characterize groundwater–surface water interactions. Results reveal sustained basin‐wide groundwater depletion over the past two decades, with accelerated losses since 2019 and during the water year 2020–2022 drought. Notably, during this recent drought period, groundwater losses were larger in the typically more resilient Upper CRB (17.5 ± 3.5 km 3 ) than in the Lower CRB (9.4 ± 6.5 km 3 ), indicating increasing vulnerability across both subbasins. Copula‐based analysis shows strong coupling between surface‐water deficits and groundwater drought probability in the Upper CRB, whereas parts of the Lower CRB exhibit weaker statistical dependence, consistent with groundwater extraction operating partly independently of surface water availability under chronically limited supply conditions. These findings provide a basin‐wide observational synthesis of groundwater–surface water dynamics and demonstrate the value of satellite‐based monitoring for diagnosing hydroclimatic stress in large managed river basins. The results highlight emerging shifts in groundwater vulnerability across the CRB and underscore the need for integrated water‐management strategies that jointly consider climatic pressures and sustained anthropogenic demand.

papers.title: Deep Learning‐Based Fusion of Hydrodynamic Model and Remote Sensing Observation for Mapping the Inundation Dynamics in Large Wetlands Under Changing Environment
papers.snippet: Wetlands play a crucial role in maintaining the global ecosystem balance, and determining the inundation dynamics is of great significance for understanding wetland ecosystems.
papers.abstract: Wetlands play a crucial role in maintaining the global ecosystem balance, and determining the inundation dynamics is of great significance for understanding wetland ecosystems. Hydrodynamic models are effective tools for mapping the inundation dynamics; however, they are affected by uncertainties arising from environmental changes, including anthropogenic pressures and land cover modifications, especially in large wetlands. To overcome hydrodynamic model limitations, this study integrated a hydrodynamic module, a remote sensing module, and a deep learning fusion module to develop an efficient approach for mapping the inundation dynamics. This approach was applied in the Poyang Lake Wetland in China, a vital conservation wetland in the Ramsar Convention. The effectiveness of this approach was verified by comparing the simulated inundation dynamics of the hydrodynamic model during the dry season. We found that the performance of the hydrodynamic model was relatively poor. In particular, the performance in the sub‐lake area was significantly inferior than the other zone, with an overall accuracy (OA, dimensionless, ranging from 0 to 1) of only 0.63–0.66. The proposed approach in this study exhibited better performance, especially in the sub‐lake area, with an OA increasing to 0.82–0.92. Furthermore, the hydrodynamic model tended to overestimate the inundation time, with the median overestimated time reaching 42–50 days. Our study provides a transferable framework that can improve the accuracy of wetland hydrological monitoring under changing environment, contribute to maintaining the ecological integrity and stability.

papers.title: A Hybrid Superdroplet–Bin Microphysics Approach Reveals How Large Salt Particles Trigger Rain in Non‐Precipitating Warm Convective Clouds
papers.snippet: This study develops a Superdroplet‐Bin hybrid microphysics scheme within the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to investigate hygroscopic seeding of warm convective clouds.
papers.abstract: This study develops a Superdroplet‐Bin hybrid microphysics scheme within the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to investigate hygroscopic seeding of warm convective clouds. The Super‐droplet method describes 3D transport, deliquescence, condensation, and collision‐coalescence growth of seeding agents or solution droplets, while the spectral bin method simulates liquid‐phase processes. Idealized simulations indicate that seeding full‐spectrum salt near cloud base can produce a maximum accumulated precipitation of 11.59 mm in 3 h. Further sensitivity experiments on seeding particle size reveal that rainfall enhancement primarily originates from particles ≥4 μm, with 5 μm yielding the most pronounced effect. This is because particles ≥4 μm can nucleate to form droplets ≥20 μm, shifting collision‐coalescence from the low‐efficiency regime below 20 μm to the high‐efficiency regime between large and drizzle‐sized droplets. The tail and rain‐embryo effects are identified as the dominant mechanisms, competition alone cannot effectively broaden the droplet spectrum or trigger precipitation.

papers.title: Watershed Characteristics Modulate the Global Response of Fractional Evapotranspiration to Wet Climate Extremes
papers.snippet: Intensifying wet extremes under continued warming threaten water security and ecosystem functioning by perturbing land–atmosphere water fluxes.
papers.abstract: Intensifying wet extremes under continued warming threaten water security and ecosystem functioning by perturbing land–atmosphere water fluxes. Yet, the watershed‐scale controls on how wet‐event intensity and duration translate into changes in fractional evapotranspiration (fET) remain poorly constrained at global scales. Here, using monthly wet climate extreme indices (CEIs) and fET across ∼986 global watersheds, we quantify CEI–fET coupling and attribute its spatial variability to watershed properties using Random Forest models and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Across event types, soil organic carbon (SOC) and groundwater table depth (GWT) consistently structure coupling regimes, indicating a robust role for soil state and subsurface storage. However, the dominant texture axis differs by extreme type: intensity‐based extremes are most strongly organized by SOC–GWT–clay regimes, consistent with pulse retention and buffering, whereas duration‐based extremes are organized by SOC–GWT–silt regimes and permafrost‐related constraints, consistent with persistence‐driven drainage and saturation sensitivity. Supported SHAP‐transition analysis identifies data‐constrained regime boundaries. Lagged correlations further reveal multi‐timescale behavior: coupling varies at short lags but tends to shift toward negative associations at longer lags, especially for duration‐based extremes. In a permafrost‐limited subset, vegetation state and topography become more prominent predictors, highlighting how cold‐region constraints alter which attributes dominate. Together, these results provide a globally consistent diagnostic framework for identifying watershed regimes where intensifying wet extremes are more likely to yield sustained evapotranspiration responses versus reduced fET sensitivity. By quantifying regime thresholds, the study offers a diagnostic framework that may inform targeted mitigation strategies and policy frameworks, such as IPCC adaptation guidelines.

papers.title: A 3D‐Based Method for Flood Depth Estimation From Social Media Images
papers.snippet: Flood depth estimation from social media images provides timely and cost‐effective observations, offering significant potential for flood monitoring and emergency response.
papers.abstract: Flood depth estimation from social media images provides timely and cost‐effective observations, offering significant potential for flood monitoring and emergency response. Existing image‐based methods typically rely on humans, vehicles, or traffic signs as scale references, however, such objects are frequently absent in real flood scenes and often yield unreliable scale information. In contrast, urban 3D models offer consistent and accurate metric references across large spatial extents. In this paper, we propose a flood depth estimation method based on urban 3D models and develop an Object‐level Coarse‐to‐Fine Matching Model that transfers metric scale from 3D models to social media images. The results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the representative 2D3D‐MATR on an urban public benchmark, increasing the inlier ratio by approximately 30% and improving the registration recall by about 16%. Building upon the matching capability, our 3D‐based flood depth estimation method generalizes across diverse flood scenarios and achieves improved accuracy, with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.164 m and a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.212 m. By transforming discrete social media data into spatially explicit, high‐accuracy flood depth maps, our method not only provides reliable support for rapid flood assessment and emergency decision‐making during events but also offers valuable data for calibrating hydraulic models post‐disaster.

papers.title: Hydropeaking Catalyzes Redox Reactions in Impacted Aquifers: A First Field Evidence
papers.snippet: Hydropeaking indicates the sudden and frequent fluctuation of river stage caused by the operation of hydropower plants. This river alteration affects numerous physical, chemical, biological, and ecohydrological processes in surface water bodies.
papers.abstract: Hydropeaking indicates the sudden and frequent fluctuation of river stage caused by the operation of hydropower plants. This river alteration affects numerous physical, chemical, biological, and ecohydrological processes in surface water bodies. The impact of hydropeaking on groundwater hydraulics has been investigated only recently through modeling and experimental studies at multiple spatial scales. This study presents new hydrological and geochemical surface water and groundwater data providing the first evidence of the impact of hydropeaking on groundwater hydrogeochemistry. To interpret these observations, we propose a conceptual model where the rapid vertical oscillation of the groundwater table acts as a pressure‐driven “geochemical pump” impacting redox conditions in the aquifer. This work has important implications for better understanding of groundwater biogeochemistry as well as for nutrient and carbon cycles.

papers.title: The OpenSat4Weather dataset: Ku-band satellite link data for precipitation monitoring
papers.snippet: The TV-SAT signals received by the ground antennas of Satellite Microwave Links (SMLs) can be opportunistically used for detecting and quantifying precipitation. Consequently, SMLs have the potential to serve as low-cost rainfall sensors complementing conventional instruments.
papers.abstract: The TV-SAT signals received by the ground antennas of Satellite Microwave Links (SMLs) can be opportunistically used for detecting and quantifying precipitation. Consequently, SMLs have the potential to serve as low-cost rainfall sensors complementing conventional instruments. However, a major challenge for opportunistic sensors, including both SMLs and their terrestrial counterpart – Commercial Microwave Links (CMLs) – is related to data ownership and accessibility constraints, possibly hindering progress in the development of processing tools and validation studies. This limitation highlights the importance of openly accessible datasets. While CML open datasets are already available, there are no large-scale SML datasets in public repositories. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenSat4Weather dataset, a comprehensive and openly accessible collection of measurements from 215 SML sensors deployed in Southern France, over a five-month period from August to December 2022. The dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16530166 (Nebuloni et al., 2025b). OpenSat4Weather also includes concurrent conventional measurements, namely, 6 min rainfall depths from 113 operational rain gauges, and radar-based estimates of rainfall intensity along each SML path. The radar data were derived from the gauge-adjusted weather radar product PANTHERE provided by Météo-France. Additionally, the dataset stores ERA5 reanalysis data of the 0 °C isotherm height for rain height estimation, which are essential for accurately converting the received signal level into rainfall intensity. In this paper, we detail the OpenSat4Weather data preparation process and draw statistics of data availability. We then provide a descriptive analysis of the dataset, including rainfall characteristics, derived from rain gauges, statistical properties of the SML received signal levels, and a comparison between SML and radar data. In addition, we illustrate examples of disturbances and anomalous patterns observed in raw SML signals. Finally, we provide some practical guidelines for processing and analyzing SML data. Our ultimate goal is to promote open research initiatives aimed at accelerating the development of SML-based applications. Enhancing rainfall monitoring by opportunistic sensors has the potential to provide substantial benefits, particularly in regions where conventional…

papers.title: Diagnosing Latent Storage Representations in LSTM Reservoir Release Policies
papers.snippet: The influence of reservoirs on the water cycle introduces significant uncertainty for hydrologic prediction. The representation of reservoirs in hydrologic models ideally must be accurate, interpretable, and transferable across sites.
papers.abstract: The influence of reservoirs on the water cycle introduces significant uncertainty for hydrologic prediction. The representation of reservoirs in hydrologic models ideally must be accurate, interpretable, and transferable across sites. Recent studies have highlighted the potential for data‐driven methods, including long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks, to accurately capture reservoir releases. However, the performance of LSTM models of reservoir releases has not yet been diagnosed on a large‐sample data set to understand whether their accuracy is physically justified. This study evaluates the ability of LSTMs to represent reservoir release policies across the continental U.S., leveraging the recently developed ResOpsUS data set. In particular, we focus on whether LSTMs can infer a latent storage representation without being provided observed storage as input. We find that in many cases the LSTM succeeds in encoding physically interpretable storage dynamics in its internal states, despite measurement errors in the data. However, the model accuracy is only weakly related to the strength of the learned storage representation; instead, it is log‐linearly related to the degree of regulation. In addition, LSTMs struggle to generalize storage dynamics and learned policies in space with pooled training. This study contributes to the growing literature on interpreting deep learning models of human‐hydrologic systems.

papers.title: Characteristic‐Aligned Control‐Volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Flood‐Wave Propagation and Roughness Estimation
papers.snippet: Physics‐informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for river hydrodynamic simulation and parameter inversion under sparse observations.
papers.abstract: Physics‐informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for river hydrodynamic simulation and parameter inversion under sparse observations. However, spatial heterogeneity in channel geometry and roughness causes strong variations in flood‐wave propagation and parameter sensitivity, challenging local conservation and joint state‐parameter estimation. This study proposes a Characteristic‐aligned Control‐volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Roughness Estimation (CC‐PINN‐RE). It constructs dynamic diamond‐shaped space‐time control volumes from local characteristic speeds of the Saint‐Venant equations, enforces mass and momentum conservation in integral form, and combines adaptive control‐volume management with local‐sensitivity‐weighted roughness regularization. The method is evaluated on three one‐dimensional channel cases of increasing complexity against strong‐form PINN‐RE and fixed‐control‐volume cvPINN‐RE. CC‐PINN‐RE achieves the lowest errors in eight of nine relative metrics for water depth, discharge, and roughness. In Case 3, where channel width, bed slope, and roughness vary spatially, it reduces the corresponding errors by 57.0%, 82.2%, and 57.3% relative to PINN‐RE and reduces the maximum absolute error in peak water depth by 69.7%. Ablation experiments with three random seeds support the contributions of the three proposed components. Observation‐deployment experiments show that increasing the number of monitoring stations is generally more effective than increasing temporal sampling frequency at individual stations. Under 0%–2% observational noise in Case 3, the model remains stable. These results indicate that CC‐PINN‐RE provides a physically consistent framework for integrating characteristic propagation, local conservation, and parameter inversion, offering a useful basis for joint hydrodynamic reconstruction and spatially varying roughness estimation in heterogeneous river channels.

papers.title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Hydrological Models
papers.snippet: The evaluation of hydrological models is essential for both model selection and reliability assessment. However, comparing predictions with observations alone is insufficient to fully characterize model behavior.
papers.abstract: The evaluation of hydrological models is essential for both model selection and reliability assessment. However, comparing predictions with observations alone is insufficient to fully characterize model behavior. This limitation is particularly relevant to deep learning (DL) models because of their complex internal structures. In risk‐averse operational settings, water managers require models whose reliability and failure modes have been carefully evaluated because unstable predictions can put critical infrastructure at risk. Motivated by the need to assess model reliability before operational deployment, we introduce and explore adversarial robustness analysis for hydrological modeling and evaluate whether small, targeted perturbations to meteorological forcings induce substantial changes in simulated discharge. We compare a physical‐conceptual model (HBV) with a deep learning‐based model (LSTM) across 1,347 German catchments using perturbations of varying magnitudes generated by the fast gradient sign method (FGSM). We find that FGSM perturbations generally reduce Kling–Gupta efficiency and increase mean squared error. However, widespread catastrophic failures under the specific FGSM perturbations are not observed, and LSTM generally exhibits less performance degradation than HBV. In the examined catchments, changes in the predicted hydrographs and time‐averaged internal model states often vary approximately linearly with perturbation magnitude, providing a compact summary of how errors grow under such perturbations. Similar patterns are observed along random perturbation directions in selected catchments, suggesting that, in those catchments, small input changes produce approximately proportional changes in model output. Overall, these findings characterize local predictive stability under controlled stress tests and motivate future studies of model robustness in real‐world operational settings.

papers.title: Quantifying Vegetation Dependence on Groundwater: Evidence From Northern China's Drylands
papers.snippet: Groundwater is a critical source for vegetation in drylands, yet the quantification of vegetation dependence on groundwater (VDG) remains underexplored. Understanding this dependence is essential for unraveling vegetation‐groundwater interactions and informing sustainable water resources management in drylands.
papers.abstract: Groundwater is a critical source for vegetation in drylands, yet the quantification of vegetation dependence on groundwater (VDG) remains underexplored. Understanding this dependence is essential for unraveling vegetation‐groundwater interactions and informing sustainable water resources management in drylands. This study constructed a vegetation response curve to depth to groundwater (DTG) by analyzing the relationship between DTG and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) at the pixel scale. A new method was developed to quantify VDG from the fitted NDVI–DTG response curve, where VDG was defined as the rate of NDVI change per unit change in normalized DTG at the inflection point of the NDVI–DTG response curve. VDG values were obtained for nine representative arid, semi‐arid, and semi‐humid regions in northern China (with an annual precipitation gradient of 200–800 mm). VDG shows pronounced spatial variation across the nine regions, with mean values decreasing from approximately 1.28 in the driest region to approximately 0.24 in the wettest region along the precipitation gradient. A strong negative correlation between annual precipitation (P) and VDG was identified (VDG = 2.08e −0.0037P ), highlighting precipitation as a dominant regulator of VDG across regions. The research provides new empirical evidence for a deeper understanding of the effects of groundwater on vegetation, and also provides strong scientific support for groundwater management and ecological restoration with various annual precipitation amounts.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Active Root Zone Storage Revealed From Hybrid Machine Learning
papers.snippet: Water within the root zone regulates water, energy, and carbon exchanges at the land‐atmosphere interface, yet the dynamically active portion of subsurface water that ecosystems mobilize for evapotranspiration (ET) remains unclear, because it represents only part of the total subsurface storage.
papers.abstract: Water within the root zone regulates water, energy, and carbon exchanges at the land‐atmosphere interface, yet the dynamically active portion of subsurface water that ecosystems mobilize for evapotranspiration (ET) remains unclear, because it represents only part of the total subsurface storage. To address this gap, we develop a catchment‐scale, ecosystem‐oriented hybrid machine learning model that integrates a parsimonious ecohydrological structure with data‐driven flexibility to infer time‐varying active root zone storage (a S rz ) as a latent state variable. Without prescribing rooting depth or soil layers, the model learns adaptive water partitioning from multi‐source observations of ET, runoff, snow, and terrestrial water storage, enabling diagnosis of both dynamic a S rz and its realized capacity. Applied across hundreds of U.S. catchments over the period 2001–2020, the framework reveals coherent spatial and hydroclimatic patterns, with a S rz peaking in transitional regions where atmospheric demand and water supply are balanced. The realized capacity reflects how belowground water access varies with long‐term hydroclimatic and substrate constraints. We further show that defining storage as a realized quantity through system dynamics improves stability and interpretability under varying observational and structural conditions. Overall, this study demonstrates how hybrid modeling can be used to diagnose ecosystem‐accessible water storage as a latent state, providing a physically consistent and observation‐informed pathway to quantify belowground processes that remain inaccessible to direct measurement and control key land‐atmosphere interactions.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Variability of Water Transit Time Distribution Across an Alpine Stream Network
papers.snippet: Water transit time (TT), the time elapsed from its entrance into a catchment and its exit through a stream section, is a useful indicator of catchment transport dynamics. Its distribution (TTD) is typically estimated at a single cross section where tracer data are available.
papers.abstract: Water transit time (TT), the time elapsed from its entrance into a catchment and its exit through a stream section, is a useful indicator of catchment transport dynamics. Its distribution (TTD) is typically estimated at a single cross section where tracer data are available. However, spatial variability of TTD is key to understanding how heterogeneous source areas contribute to solute and water quality dynamics. Here, we investigate how TTD varies along a stream network. To this end, we analyzed stable isotopes in rainfall (three stations) and streamwater (eight sampling sites) in the Valfredda network draining an alpine catchment. To quantitatively analyze the data, we developed a spatially explicit model of TTD based on StorAge Selection (SAS) functions. The catchment is discretized into subcatchment units, each characterized by distinct SAS functions. Subcatchment TTDs are routed through the network to estimate TTDs at every cross section. Parameter estimation relies on a hierarchical Bayesian framework, which ensures consistency across subcatchments while allowing heterogeneity. Results indicate that streamflow preferentially samples older water from storage, with only a limited number of flow events triggering young water release. Despite pronounced heterogeneity in geomorphology and land cover, the inferred SAS functions exhibit only mild spatial variability. Differences in TTDs are driven primarily by variations in precipitation phase (liquid vs. solid) and the timing of snowmelt‐driven fluxes, rather than by intrinsic differences in mixing mechanisms. Both sources of variability are explicitly represented within the proposed framework, highlighting its general applicability to reveal transport dynamics at the catchment scale.

papers.title: Physics‐Informed Fusion Learning for Nowcasting Fault Detection of Hydrological Multi Sensor Network
papers.snippet: Urban flood monitoring demands timely, reliable decisions under urgent and often unseen conditions. However, faults in sensor networks can undermine response, leading to human and economic losses.
papers.abstract: Urban flood monitoring demands timely, reliable decisions under urgent and often unseen conditions. However, faults in sensor networks can undermine response, leading to human and economic losses. To address these issues, we propose a Nowcasting Physics‐Informed (NPI) model for fault detection in streamflow sensors, with a 100‐min memory window at 2‐min resolution. A Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) consumes fused features from measured signals and Storm Water Management Model simulator outputs to produce end‐of‐window fault probabilities. To ensure operational reliability, a lightweight per‐sensor eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) stage calibrates the LSTM score using window‐local statistics of the measurement. In this study, we investigate whether and to what extent fusing a physical model with sensor data improves fault detection, and whether per‐sensor threshold calibration matters. Our results indicated yes. The Area under the precision–recall curve (AUC‐PR) was improved by 3.7%–12.5% over the physics‐informed model compared to baseline non‐physics‐informed learning. In addition, post‐hoc calibration improved AUC‐PR by an additional 0.2%–2.3%. Across five cross‐validation folds, F1‐score (F1) increased from 0.75 for the non‐physics LSTM baseline to 0.83 with calibration, and further to 0.88 for the physics informed model. Adding post‐hoc calibration to the physics informed model yielded the best result at 0.90. The NPI is causal and auditable, exporting calibrated probabilities and binary alerts for direct operator use without retraining the LSTM, and offers a practical template for warning systems and training strategies that remain robust to unseen conditions.

papers.title: A monthly 250 m Vegetation Drought Resistance Index (VDRI) dataset for China from 2000 to 2022
papers.snippet: Global warming is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme droughts, threatening terrestrial ecosystem structure and function.
papers.abstract: Global warming is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme droughts, threatening terrestrial ecosystem structure and function. However, existing indices often fail to provide a comprehensive representation of the water cycle, and high-resolution datasets for characterizing vegetation responses to drought remain limited. To address this gap, we first developed a monthly Vertical Composite Drought Index (VCDI) by integrating precipitation, surface runoff, soil moisture, and groundwater storage anomalies. This index summarizes multidimensional water constraints across the “atmosphere-surface-subsurface” continuum and captures cumulative effects of drought across multiple timescales. Furthermore, VCDI, land surface temperature, and vegetation greenness were combined to produce a monthly Vegetation Drought Resistance Index (VDRI) dataset for China at 250 m resolution from 2000 to 2022. Multi-source evaluations indicate that VDRI provides spatially detailed and temporally consistent information on vegetation conditions under concurrent hydroclimatic and thermal stress. The datasets support ecosystem assessment, ecological drought monitoring, wildfire risk analysis, and benchmarking for drought-impact studies and related ecological models.

papers.title: A 256-year daily rainfall record reveals multiscale rainy-season variability and emerging hydroclimatic hazard over northern East Asia
papers.snippet: Monsoon rainy seasons shape water supply and flood hazard across northern East Asia, but their long-term variability remains poorly understood because few daily rainfall records extend beyond the instrumental era.
papers.abstract: Monsoon rainy seasons shape water supply and flood hazard across northern East Asia, but their long-term variability remains poorly understood because few daily rainfall records extend beyond the instrumental era. Here, we reconstruct rainy-season onset, retreat, and duration from a 256-year daily precipitation record for Seoul (1770–2025), providing an unusually long view of seasonal monsoon behavior. The reconstruction reveals structured quasi-decadal to multidecadal variability in rainy-season duration, indicating that recent rainy-season lengthening over northern East Asia is consistent with the latest positive excursion of a recurrent multidecadal modulation rather than a purely isolated modern anomaly. Coupled with warming-associated intensification of extreme rainfall, this prolonged-duration phase has elevated the compound-hazard probability, with recent probability peaks exceeding the long-term mean of ∼25% in Seoul. Exploratory near-term outlooks suggest that rainy-season duration in northern East Asia is likely to remain prolonged toward mid-century, sustaining heightened compound hydroclimatic hazard when seasonally extended overlaps with intensified event-scale rainfall.

papers.title: Intensification of East Asian summer extreme precipitation under a net-zero anthropogenic CO 2 emission scenario
papers.snippet: Global warming has intensified extreme precipitation, a trend projected to continue as warming persists. However, how extreme precipitation characteristics respond to global warming mitigation strategies remains poorly understood.
papers.abstract: Global warming has intensified extreme precipitation, a trend projected to continue as warming persists. However, how extreme precipitation characteristics respond to global warming mitigation strategies remains poorly understood. This study examines East Asian summer extreme precipitation responses under a net-zero anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emission scenario. Despite substantial cooling over East Asia following atmospheric CO 2 concentration decline, the intensity of extreme precipitation events continues to increase for about 30 years and does not subsequently weaken. This counterintuitive result arises mainly from intensified upward motion during extreme precipitation events, driven by enhanced baroclinicity and strengthening of the upper-tropospheric jet, which together overcompensate the cooling effect. These are essentially due to the hysteresis in the Atlantic (i.e., Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation slowdown), Southern (i.e., sustained warming), and Pacific (i.e., El Niño–like warming) Oceans. Our findings highlight that achieving net-zero anthropogenic CO 2 emissions is insufficient to mitigate intensifying extreme rainfall events in the densely populated East Asian countries.

papers.title: Wildfires diminish vegetation control on surface runoff
papers.snippet: Wildfires are increasingly reshaping global terrestrial ecosystems, yet their impacts on the fundamental coupling between vegetation and the hydrological cycle remain poorly understood.
papers.abstract: Wildfires are increasingly reshaping global terrestrial ecosystems, yet their impacts on the fundamental coupling between vegetation and the hydrological cycle remain poorly understood. Here, we present a global-scale assessment of how wildfire disturbances alter the sensitivity of surface runoff to vegetation dynamics using multidecadal satellite observations and reanalysis datasets. We developed a spatially explicit framework to quantify pre- and postfire runoff-vegetation sensitivity across climatic gradients and fire regimes. We show a widespread and systematic weakening of vegetation control on runoff after wildfires, indicating a fundamental decoupling of hydrology-vegetation interactions. This attenuation is notably modulated by aridity and fire intensity, with the most pronounced sensitivity losses occurring in fragile drylands. These findings expose a critical blind spot in traditional hydrological models that overlook disturbance-driven vegetation shifts. Our study provides a mechanistic understanding of how compound climate-fire perturbations accelerate terrestrial water flux instability, suggesting that increasing fire frequency will exacerbate ecosystem vulnerability and threaten water security in a warming world.

papers.title: The influence of lakes and reservoirs on estimated flood peaks at hourly vs. daily timescale in the Alps
papers.snippet: Water bodies such as lakes and reservoirs can play a crucial role in reducing estimated flood peaks, at both daily and hourly time resolution.
papers.abstract: Water bodies such as lakes and reservoirs can play a crucial role in reducing estimated flood peaks, at both daily and hourly time resolution. While the effect of water bodies on flood peaks has been demonstrated in the past at different time resolutions, it remains unclear how water bodies affect the ratio between estimated daily and hourly quantiles, that is, to which degree their attenuation effect is scale dependent. Here, we analyse how water bodies influence this ratio using two approaches: (1) by comparing estimated daily and hourly flood peak quantiles upstream and downstream of reservoirs of four local case studies, and (2) by comparing daily and hourly flood peak quantiles across a large sample of catchments in Switzerland with various degrees of water-body influence. Our results show that reservoirs dampen hourly peak discharge much more strongly than daily peak discharge, which leads to similar daily and hourly flood peaks downstream of reservoirs. Specifically, our case study analysis highlights that (sub-)hourly peak discharge is attenuated by up to 70 % downstream of reservoirs during flood events with a 10-year return period. We also find that the attenuation effect is particularly pronounced in catchments that are heavily influenced by water bodies, i.e. those catchments where more than 60 % of the area contributes to water body inflow. This implies that daily flood peaks are a good proxy for hourly peaks in strongly regulated catchments in contrast to natural ones. We conclude that considering water body influence on flood peaks is crucial to understand the similarity between daily and hourly flood peaks downstream of water bodies. This suggests that water body influence should also be considered in large-sample studies for which the exact influence may be unknown, and quantified using suitable metrics such as the fraction of the total catchment above the water body.

papers.title: The influence of vapor pressure deficit changes on global terrestrial evapotranspiration
papers.snippet: Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) has been widely recognized as a key driver of uncertainty in future global evapotranspiration ( E ) trends.
papers.abstract: Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) has been widely recognized as a key driver of uncertainty in future global evapotranspiration ( E ) trends. Accurately characterizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of VPD and elucidating its influence on terrestrial E are critical for understanding land–atmosphere water and energy feedback processes under climate warming. However, previous studies have largely focused on the physiological regulation of plant transpiration ( E t ) at the leaf or canopy scale, leaving the quantitative understanding of VPD– E interactions at the global scale incomplete. By integrating multi-source remote sensing products and reanalysis datasets, this study quantitatively evaluates the role of VPD in regulating global terrestrial E variability. The main findings are as follows: (1) Approximately 60.7 % of global land area exhibits positive apparent sensitivity of E to VPD, with a global mean sensitivity of 293.3±62.3 mm hPa −1 , and stronger responses observed in warm and humid regions. (2) VPD is positively correlated with E t overall, particularly in mid-to-high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, whereas its correlation with bare soil evaporation ( E b ) is weaker and tends to be negative in water-limited regions. (3) The VPD– E relationship exhibits a pronounced aridity-dependent threshold, which decreases progressively from arid (1.90 kPa) and semi-arid (1.46 kPa) regions to semi-humid (0.49 kPa) and humid (0.47 kPa) regions. Further path analysis reveals that VPD regulates E through interconnected pathways involving atmospheric demand, soil moisture, vegetation physiology, and energy supply, with an overall negative net effect on E . This study clarifies the dominant pathways and regional heterogeneity of VPD– E interactions at the global scale, providing quantitative constraints for predicting the response of the terrestrial water cycle to increasing atmospheric aridity.

papers.title: Catchment hydrologic function is widely time-variant
papers.snippet: Catchment hydrologic function describes how meteorological conditions are transformed into streamflow. Whether this transformation is stable or varies from event to event, and what controls that variability, remains unknown at the global scale, limiting confidence in flood-risk and water-security assessments.
papers.abstract: Catchment hydrologic function describes how meteorological conditions are transformed into streamflow. Whether this transformation is stable or varies from event to event, and what controls that variability, remains unknown at the global scale, limiting confidence in flood-risk and water-security assessments. Here, we analyze about 1.7 million runoff-producing events across 4838 catchments on six continents. We classify each event by its water-input type (rain, snowmelt, or rain-on-snow) and by its antecedent soil moisture (dry, moderate, or wet). These two descriptors together define the event’s hydro-meteorological conditions. We summarize each catchment’s dominant hydro-meteorological event type in the dormant and growing seasons separately, and find a wide diversity of dominant types across the global catchment population. We then quantify, for each catchment, the extent of event-to-event time-variance in the precipitation–streamflow transfer function that represents catchment hydrologic function. Time-variant catchment hydrologic function is pervasive: 95.6% of catchments in the dormant season and 99.0% in the growing season show moderate to strong event-to-event variation, and even catchments experiencing highly similar hydro-meteorological conditions across events remain functionally time-variant. Within-catchment spatial heterogeneity in hydro-meteorological conditions modulates this variation. Greater time-variance in hydrologic function is associated with greater event-to-event variation in a catchment’s runoff response.

papers.title: Agricultural Drought Response in Temperate Climates Requires Institutional Development and Coordination to Support Adaptation
papers.snippet: Droughts and dry periods represent a novel and emerging threat to agriculture in historically water rich, temperate regions, such as the Northeast United States. Water governance institutions to manage water quantity in these regions are underdeveloped in the context of current needs.
papers.abstract: Droughts and dry periods represent a novel and emerging threat to agriculture in historically water rich, temperate regions, such as the Northeast United States. Water governance institutions to manage water quantity in these regions are underdeveloped in the context of current needs. In this study, we examine the state of Maine as a case study in drought institutions in a historically water‐rich region. Specifically, we review the institutional landscape for drought resilience and resistance for Maine agriculture and identify the gaps that may be hindering agricultural adaptation. Through focus groups with farmers and agricultural advisors, we find: (a) There are few quasi‐governmental organizations and programs dedicated to agricultural drought‐adaptation; rather farmers rely upon mostly federal, state, and non‐governmental regional programs and policies that are non‐drought specific in nature; and (b) there is a need for articulated and persistent coordination between federal‐state‐local organizations and programs, to ensure vertical and horizontal integration and complementarity. In the absence of drought‐specific institutions that coordinate across scales, there is the potential for ineffective drought adaptation and maladaptation in Maine and other temperate regions. This could result in wasted public and private resources, ineffective use of natural resources, and inequitable or otherwise socially undesirable outcomes. Our research adds to the growing body of evidence showing that, even in temperate and historically water‐rich regions, drought is a threat to agricultural viability. Here, we outline the need for institutional coordination around drought‐adaptation to facilitate strategic program development.

papers.title: SWOT‐Fitted River Bathymetry for Global Hydrodynamic Models
papers.snippet: We present a robust, global method to reconcile absolute water surface elevations (WSE) from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission with a large‐scale hydrodynamic model by iteratively correcting river bathymetry.
papers.abstract: We present a robust, global method to reconcile absolute water surface elevations (WSE) from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission with a large‐scale hydrodynamic model by iteratively correcting river bathymetry. After removing sensor and representativeness bias, we update riverbed elevations under DEM and min‐depth feasibility constraints and interpolate corrections along reaches. Applied worldwide at 0.05° resolution over 2023–2025, the approach reduces the global median absolute WSE bias (3.10 m → 0.18 m), preserving the same global median correlation (0.38). A modest ∼4% increase in the standard deviation ratio (1.07 → 1.11) indicates slight variance inflation. Independent evaluation over 2015–2025 at 16,746 Hydroweb sites and 2123 GRDC gauges, restricted to reaches with updated beds, confirms substantially reduced bias, negligible change in both correlation and variance, and no significant change in global median discharge skill. When combined with models, this bias‐aware bathymetry will enable a refined numerical representation of floods globally.

papers.title: Dispersed Urban Expansion Amplifies Land Surface Evapotranspiration Loss
papers.snippet: The expansion of impervious surfaces (IS) substantially modifies urban water cycles and local climate regimes by suppressing evapotranspiration (ET), thereby affecting the sustainability of human settlements.
papers.abstract: The expansion of impervious surfaces (IS) substantially modifies urban water cycles and local climate regimes by suppressing evapotranspiration (ET), thereby affecting the sustainability of human settlements. However, most existing studies have emphasized the effects of IS quantity or coverage, while it remains unclear how different spatial patterns of urban expansion—dispersed versus compact—differentially regulate ET loss, as well as the extent of their respective impacts. This study integrates machine learning, interpretable artificial intelligence, and landscape pattern analysis to disentangle, with 256 cities in China as the research area, for the first time, the role of IS spatial expansion mode in regulating ET. Our results reveal that the suppressive effect of IS on ET weakens progressively from humid to arid regions and that its contribution to ET reduction follows a logarithmic growth pattern (all R 2 > 0.6), intensifying most rapidly during initial urbanization. This early‐stage sensitivity makes the initial choice of spatial expansion modes critical. Our causal analysis confirms that leap‐frogging expansion—characterized by high dispersion and low connectivity—exerts the strongest per‐unit‐area suppression, reducing ET by 93.1 ± 48.4% more than compact, interior‐filling expansion. In humid coastal megacities, each 10% increase in impervious surface percentage under this dispersed pattern reduces ET by 28.2 mm/yr. These findings underscore the critical role played by the spatial pattern of urban expansion in hydroclimatic regulation and provide a quantitative basis for designing climate‐resilient cities that sustain both development and ecological functions.

papers.title: Global Multi-Index Drought (GMID): a multiscalar high-resolution dataset from 1980 to near present
papers.snippet: Drought assessment is an extremely complex task that relies on high-quality datasets, posing a major challenge for scientists and water managers.
papers.abstract: Drought assessment is an extremely complex task that relies on high-quality datasets, posing a major challenge for scientists and water managers. Here, we present the Global Multi-Index Drought (GMID), a multiscalar high-resolution dataset that includes five standardised drought indices: the Standardised Precipitation Index (SPI), the Evaporative Drought Demand Index (EDDI), the Standardised Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), the Standardised Evapotranspiration Deficit Index (SEDI), and the Standardised Vapor Pressure Deficit Index (SVPDI). This dataset is available globally at multiple time scales (1- to 12-, 18-, 24-, 48-month) for the period 1980–2024, with high spatial (0.1°) and temporal (weekly and monthly) resolution. The GMID dataset contains two versions of the drought indices; one generated using a traditional single-distribution approach, and another using a new flexible-distribution approach allowing the selection of probability distributions providing the best-fitting normalised series in each case. GMID adds significant value to previous drought data products through its high resolution and flexible multi-index nature, representing a comprehensive and robust long-term dataset for drought (and flash drought) assessment at the global scale.

papers.title: Global Assessment of SWOT River Discharge Representation at Channel Bifurcations
papers.snippet: SWOT river discharge products rely on the SWOT River Database (SWORD), designed mainly for single‐thread channels. We assess how well SWORD represents ∼65,000 river bifurcations from the Global River Topology (GRIT) network.
papers.abstract: SWOT river discharge products rely on the SWOT River Database (SWORD), designed mainly for single‐thread channels. We assess how well SWORD represents ∼65,000 river bifurcations from the Global River Topology (GRIT) network. SWORD geographically intersects both downstream branches at 88.2% of bifurcations, but only 2.0% of these have distinct reach IDs per branch. At structurally usable bifurcations, summed branch discharge exceeds the upstream value by a median factor of 2.1 in every algorithm tested, and the closure error is independent of branch width asymmetry. A width‐based redistribution ( Q ∝ W 1.52 ) enforces closure by construction; at the Athabasca–Embarras bifurcation, when anchored to the upstream gauge discharge and using Landsat‐derived branch widths, the redistribution matches the gauged Embarras flow fraction ( Q EM / Q upstream ) within 0.004 whereas SoS V3 underestimates it by 0.089. Improved multi‐channel topology in SWORD‐like frameworks remains the longer‐term path to branch‐resolved discharge.

papers.title: Hydrological Extremes Increase Water‐Resource Constraints Under Climate Change
papers.snippet: Hydrological extremes are projected to intensify under climate change, yet their implications for water scarcity remain poorly understood. We use a multi‐model ensemble to assess how changes in hydrological low and high extremes will constrain renewable water for human use across 520 major river basins worldwide.
papers.abstract: Hydrological extremes are projected to intensify under climate change, yet their implications for water scarcity remain poorly understood. We use a multi‐model ensemble to assess how changes in hydrological low and high extremes will constrain renewable water for human use across 520 major river basins worldwide. We evaluate trends in two metrics of water availability: (a) annual lowest monthly runoff, and (b) annual accessible runoff, a conceptual indicator defined as total runoff excluding extreme high flows typically released rapidly for flood control. More than 40% of river basins are projected to experience declines in both metrics during 2015–2100. Mediterranean and several scattered basins are identified as hotspots where runoff reductions compound existing water scarcity. Scenario comparison shows that low emission mitigates, though do not fully eliminate, these declines, highlighting hydrological co‐benefits of climate mitigation. The novelty lies in explicitly incorporating hydrological extremes into water availability assessment.

papers.title: The 2023–2024 El Niño as a Preview of Future Tropical Forest Climate
papers.snippet: Tropical forests are an important component of the global carbon cycle. Increasingly frequent droughts and heatwaves are undermining their resilience, with far‐reaching impacts on local livelihoods and on regional and global hydrological cycles.
papers.abstract: Tropical forests are an important component of the global carbon cycle. Increasingly frequent droughts and heatwaves are undermining their resilience, with far‐reaching impacts on local livelihoods and on regional and global hydrological cycles. El Niño events, recurring climate patterns that lead to dry and hot conditions across multiple tropical regions, have always influenced these dynamics, but the 2023–2024 El Niño produced extreme droughts and heatwaves that exceeded the typical El Niño footprint. Here, we place the 2023–2024 El Niño in both past (2000–2024) and future (2025–2100) climatic contexts across pantropical forests. We assess its climatic magnitude using ensembles of reanalyses, satellite climate products, and Earth System Models. Climate anomalies over 2000–2024 show that three quarters of pantropical forests experienced, on average, 6 months of compound droughts and heatwaves during 2023–2024. Based on future climate projections, most tropical forest regions will reach high probabilities of experiencing 2023–2024‐like temperatures on an annual basis, while the probability of similar droughts is expected to increase mostly in Amazonian forests. These results indicate that the 2023–2024 El Niño may have presented a preview of future tropical forest conditions, which can only be prevented by rapid and drastic reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions.

papers.title: Improved estimation of net ecosystem CO 2 exchange over North America using LSTM-based flux upscaling (2001–2021)
papers.snippet: Accurate estimation of regional-scale terrestrial carbon budgets is of great importance but remains challenging. With particular advantages, the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network method shows potential for improving regional carbon budget upscaling estimations.
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of regional-scale terrestrial carbon budgets is of great importance but remains challenging. With particular advantages, the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network method shows potential for improving regional carbon budget upscaling estimations. Here, using LSTM, we upscaled regional net ecosystem carbon exchange (NEE) with available flux tower measurements and satellite land surface observations in North America. With well-established ecosystem-specific LSTMs, we produced monthly NEE at a spatial resolution of 0.1 ° ×0.1 ° over 2001–2021 (labelled as MemoryFlux). Unlike existing upscaling estimates, our dataset properly identified the Midwest Corn Belt as a region of large seasonal carbon uptake during the peak growing season, a feature revealed by previous top-down studies and recognized as a model benchmark. Moreover, the seasonal variations in NEE estimated by MemoryFlux were strongly correlated with those from independent atmospheric inversions, including the ensemble mean of the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 Model Intercomparison Project (OCO-2 v10 MIP; r =0.96, p <0.001) and CarbonTracker2022 (CT2022) ( r =0.97, p <0.001). The mean annual NEE was estimated at −1.27 ± 0.12 Pg C yr −1 , which was closer in magnitude to inversions (−0.83 to −0.70 Pg C yr −1 ) than existing upscaling estimates (−3.30 to −1.68 Pg C yr −1 ). In addition, MemoryFlux captured spatial NEE anomaly patterns associated with six selected severe drought and flood events. We further found that explicitly incorporating historical predictor information improved the representation of NEE interannual variability and spatial anomalies associated with climate extremes. MemoryFlux provides an improved bottom-up estimation of North American NEE and shows greater consistency in magnitude with independent atmospheric inversion estimates than several existing EC-based upscaling products. The MemoryFlux dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20482274 (Huang and He, 2026).

papers.title: Probable Maximum Precipitation Estimation Under Climate Change: Addressing Sampling and Bias Correction Uncertainties Using Large Ensemble Climate Simulations
papers.snippet: This study presents an integrated framework for estimating Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP)‐equivalent return levels under climate change, addressing two critical challenges: sampling uncertainty for rare events and the validation of bias correction under different global warming scenarios.
papers.abstract: This study presents an integrated framework for estimating Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP)‐equivalent return levels under climate change, addressing two critical challenges: sampling uncertainty for rare events and the validation of bias correction under different global warming scenarios. Leveraging large regional climate model ensembles, the framework combines spatial transposition, based on L‐moment homogeneity, with ensemble pooling to expand the effective sample size to nearly 10,000 independent annual maxima per location. Results show that spatial transposition significantly reduces uncertainty in rare‐event return levels, narrowing 95% confidence intervals by over 60% for the 10,000‐year event. Improvements were most notable in the upper tail, where empirical quantiles closely matched Generalized Extreme Value fits due to increased parameter stability from the expanded sample size. Subsequently, three bias correction techniques, CDF‐transform (CDFt), Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM), and Quantile Mapping (QM), were applied to CanRCM4‐LE and evaluated against CRCM5‐LE using a pseudo‐observation framework that allowed assessment under different warming scenarios. CDFt consistently provided the best agreement with distributional properties and empirical quantiles, followed by QDM. Using the best‐performing bias correction method applied to CRCM5‐LE with ERA5 reanalysis serving as the observational reference, PMP‐equivalent return levels at grid cells corresponding to 2,730 dam locations across Northeastern North America, show spatially coherent increases, with median 100,000‐year return levels rising by ∼57% under +1.5°C and ∼77% under +3.0°C warming. Broader spatial patterns mirror this intensification, underscoring the thermodynamic drivers of future extremes. The framework enables robust, reproducible PMP estimation and supports adaptive design strategies for critical infrastructure under climate uncertainty.

papers.title: Structure–Function Coherent Coarsening for Cross‐Resolution Ecohydrological Modeling
papers.snippet: Ecohydrological models are increasingly applied in regional scenario‐based studies, yet their cross‐resolution application remains constrained by high computational costs of fine‐resolution simulations and by structural inconsistencies introduced during scale transfer.
papers.abstract: Ecohydrological models are increasingly applied in regional scenario‐based studies, yet their cross‐resolution application remains constrained by high computational costs of fine‐resolution simulations and by structural inconsistencies introduced during scale transfer. We propose a Structure–Function Coherent Coarsening (SFCC) framework that improves the preservation of hydrological structure and functional heterogeneity during model input coarsening. Using the VELMA model in 24 subbasins of the Salish Sea Basin, USA, we evaluate coarsening strategies for three input types: (a) DEMs coarsened with a Hydro‐Aware approach that better preserves drainage topology; (b) land cover and soil type data sets coarsened with function‐preserving methods ( Auto‐Weight and Auto‐Reassign ) that retain small but process‐dominant classes; and (c) initial conditions coarsened with Hydro‐Aware , Landcover‐Aware , and Soil‐Aware strategies to improve temporal stability. Results show that the Hydro‐Aware method better preserves watershed morphology and yields more consistent runoff and nitrate loss predictions across resolutions than mean‐based coarsening. For categorical inputs, the function‐preserving methods can reduce the dominant‐class bias of majority aggregation, particularly in basins where small, high‐impact patches drive nitrogen export. Long‐term simulations show that hydrological variables stabilize quickly, whereas biogeochemical variables stabilize more slowly. In both cases, differences caused by coarsening decrease over time and eventually level off. This suggests that preserving both structural consistency and functional heterogeneity can help maintain stable model behavior over time. By operating directly at the data‐input level, SFCC improves integration of multi‐source data sets while retaining high‐resolution information. It supports cross‐scale simulation, calibration, and model integration, and provides a scalable foundation for regional scenario analysis.

papers.title: Quantifying Groundwater–Surface Water Exchange on a River Island: A Comparative Analysis of Direct and Indirect Methods
papers.snippet: Groundwater–surface water exchange is a key hydrological process that governs river water quality and aquatic ecosystems. However, the quantification of such exchange remains uncertain, especially within river island aquifers where exchange processes are highly heterogeneous.
papers.abstract: Groundwater–surface water exchange is a key hydrological process that governs river water quality and aquatic ecosystems. However, the quantification of such exchange remains uncertain, especially within river island aquifers where exchange processes are highly heterogeneous. In this study, direct seepage meter measurements and indirect Darcy‐based estimates of exchange fluxes were compared under consistent spatiotemporal conditions within the aquifer of Jungsa Island, a river island in the lower West Nakdong River, South Korea. At the downstream low‐permeability site (SP‐3), Darcy‐based exchange fluxes ranged from −2.14 × 10 −5 to 1.15 × 10 −5 m/hr. Owing to these small magnitudes, net intrusion and discharge were not distinguishable. However, seepage meter measurements consistently indicated intrusion of surface water into the island aquifer, with fluxes ranging from −8.46 × 10 −4 to −1.94 × 10 −4 m/hr. At the upstream high‐permeability site (SP‐6), seepage meter measurements captured both transient groundwater discharge during short measurement periods and sustained surface water intrusion during longer measurements. Darcy‐based estimates at this site consistently indicated intrusion, indicating that both methods showed the same flow direction during longer measurements. Consequently, Darcy‐based approaches may underestimate exchange fluxes under low‐permeability conditions. These findings suggest that short‐term monitoring is favorable for capturing immediate, transient flow dynamics, whereas extended continuous measurements help buffer short‐term fluctuations to provide a more representative estimate of daily integrated exchange. Ultimately, by establishing a methodological framework that accounts for localized riverbed heterogeneity, this study provides practical guidelines for optimizing field investigation strategies in complex riparian environments.

papers.title: HydroDiffusion: Diffusion‐Based Probabilistic Streamflow Forecasting With a State Space Backbone
papers.snippet: Recent advances have introduced diffusion models for probabilistic streamflow forecasting, demonstrating strong early flood‐warning skill. However, current implementations rely on Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) backbones and discrete‐time diffusion formulations.
papers.abstract: Recent advances have introduced diffusion models for probabilistic streamflow forecasting, demonstrating strong early flood‐warning skill. However, current implementations rely on Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) backbones and discrete‐time diffusion formulations. This leaves unresolved whether more advanced sequence‐modeling architectures and continuous‐time diffusion formulations can improve probabilistic streamflow forecasting. In this study, we developed HydroDiffusion, a diffusion‐based probabilistic forecasting framework integrating a decoder‐only state space model (SSM) backbone with a continuous‐time score‐based diffusion formulation. HydroDiffusion is evaluated across 531 watersheds in the contiguous United States (CONUS) in the CAMELS data set. We benchmark HydroDiffusion against two diffusion baselines with LSTM backbones, as well as the recently proposed Diffusion‐based Runoff Model (DRUM). Results show that HydroDiffusion achieves the strongest nowcast accuracy when driven by observed meteorological forcings. Moreover, HydroDiffusion delivers higher deterministic and probabilistic forecast skill than its LSTM‐based counterpart in operational forecasting. Attribution analysis further reveals that the SSM backbone excels in humid, densely vegetated, storage‐dominated watersheds with strong hydrologic memory, while its advantage becomes limited in arid regions and hydrologically complex systems such as karst and prairie pothole basins. These results establish HydroDiffusion as an effective generative modeling framework for medium‐range streamflow forecasting, providing both a new modeling benchmark and a foundation for future research on probabilistic hydrologic prediction at continental scales.

papers.title: How Data Uncertainty Influences Estimates of Root Zone Water Storage Capacity
papers.snippet: Root zone water storage capacity () sets the lower limit on the water available to plants and is critical for modeling terrestrial water and carbon fluxes. Due to subsurface heterogeneity in soils, roots, and geology, in‐situ measurements of are infeasible at regional to global scales.
papers.abstract: Root zone water storage capacity () sets the lower limit on the water available to plants and is critical for modeling terrestrial water and carbon fluxes. Due to subsurface heterogeneity in soils, roots, and geology, in‐situ measurements of are infeasible at regional to global scales. Instead, is often estimated using a water balance approach—calculating the difference between precipitation and evapotranspiration to approximate water deficits. This method can be applied using diverse data sets, including those from eddy covariance, satellite remote sensing, reanalysis, and land surface model outputs. However, each data product contains its own uncertainties, and the influence of data set choice on estimates has not been quantified. In this study, we assess the uncertainty in estimates across 90 FLUXNET sites in the continental United States with at least 5 years of data, comparing results from six different precipitation and evapotranspiration data sets. We find substantial variation in estimates across data sets, sites, and land cover types, with particularly high uncertainty for values exceeding 500 mm. Much of this uncertainty can be attributed to differences among evapotranspiration products rather than random errors. Our analysis shows that single data set approaches to quantifying underestimate the variability that emerges when multiple data sets are considered, especially in the Western US. These results underscore the need to account for data‐driven uncertainty when estimating subsurface water storage and provide a foundation for improving model parameterizations of ecosystem drought response and land‐atmosphere interactions.

papers.title: Assessment of bias correction techniques for satellite soil moisture data assimilation in the dry season of Southeastern South America
papers.snippet: Estimation of surface soil moisture (SSM) is fundamental for hydrological monitoring and agricultural management, particularly in drought-prone regions such as central–northeastern Argentina. Data assimilation provides a robust approach for estimating SSM by integrating land surface models with remote sensing data.
papers.abstract: Estimation of surface soil moisture (SSM) is fundamental for hydrological monitoring and agricultural management, particularly in drought-prone regions such as central–northeastern Argentina. Data assimilation provides a robust approach for estimating SSM by integrating land surface models with remote sensing data. Satellite missions such as SMAP and SMOS deliver global SSM products; however, these observations often exhibit systematic biases arising from instrument noise, indirect measurements, and temporal and spatial heterogeneities. Since standard data assimilation techniques assume unbiased observations, bias correction is required to ensure optimal assimilation. This work evaluates off-line observation bias-correction methods within a land data assimilation framework based on the Noah-MP land surface model and an ensemble Kalman filter, focusing on the 2022 dry season in the endorheic Pampas region. During dry conditions, SSM probability density functions differ significantly among soil textures within the bin. To address sampling errors in cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching, we propose an approach in which climatological statistics are computed using homogeneous soil texture pixels, and a 45-day moving temporal window is applied to smooth CDF evolution. The proposed method is compared with standard CDF matching and normal deviate scaling. Results indicate that improved statistical sampling in CDF matching produces a measurable impact on SSM estimates, particularly during dry periods. It shows better agreement with independent in-situ soil measurements than standard CDF matching, provided that the soil texture classifications at the in-situ site and in the model grid cell are consistent.

papers.title: The ability of LSTM to model snowmelt versus rainfall generated floods
papers.snippet: One of the most important skills of hydrological models is to simulate timing and magnitude of flood events. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are currently among the most successful models for streamflow and flood prediction over large regions.
papers.abstract: One of the most important skills of hydrological models is to simulate timing and magnitude of flood events. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are currently among the most successful models for streamflow and flood prediction over large regions. In snow-influenced catchments, which typically comprise a minority in large-scale studies, floods are generated by two distinctly different processes, snowmelt and rainfall. The applicability of hydrological models in such regions is therefore dependent on their ability to represent both types of floods. Nevertheless, flood evaluations of LSTM taking different flood-generating processes into account are currently lacking. This study fills this gap by evaluating the ability of LSTM to model flood peak characteristics separately for snowmelt and rainfall generated floods. The trained LSTM model successfully simulated streamflow time series across the 103 evaluated catchments, with average NSE of 0.84 and average KGE of 0.86 over the unseen evaluation period. LSTM exhibited better performance in the majority of the catchments in terms of flood peak timing and magnitude for both rainfall and snowmelt generated floods when compared to the operational hydrological model in the region (HBV) used as a benchmark. LSTM had a 27 pp higher percentage of correctly simulated peak days for rainfall generated floods as compared to snowmelt generated floods, similar to what was found for HBV (29 pp). LSTM's ability to simulate flood peak magnitudes was similar for the different flood types, with percent errors within 20 % for close to half of the events. False alarm rate and probability of detection results were similar for snowmelt and rainfall generated events, both slightly better than those of mixed events. LSTM outperformed HBV in 70 %–91 % of the catchments in terms of flood peak timing and magnitude for snowmelt and rainfall generated floods. The largest improvements in flood peak magnitudes were found for rainfall generated events, in particular for catchments where HBV exhibited high (>40 % ) absolute errors. Overall, our findings bring confidence that LSTM can improve hydrological services in regions subject to both snowmelt and rainfall generated floods.

papers.title: Distinct Dependencies of Tropical Cyclone Inner‐Core and Outer‐Region Precipitation on Translation Speed and Intensity
papers.snippet: This study analyzes how tropical cyclone (TC) precipitation in the inner core (IC) and outer region (OR) varies with translation speed and storm intensity using satellite‐derived precipitation data.
papers.abstract: This study analyzes how tropical cyclone (TC) precipitation in the inner core (IC) and outer region (OR) varies with translation speed and storm intensity using satellite‐derived precipitation data. Inner core precipitation initially increases with translation speed but decreases at higher speeds, while OR precipitation increases nearly linearly with translation speed. Inner core precipitation is strongly linked to TC intensity, both with and without conditioning on translation speed, whereas OR precipitation increases with intensity primarily for stronger storms. As translation speed increases, the location of maximum precipitation shifts toward the forward‐left quadrant in the Northern Hemisphere, accompanied by a pronounced increase in rainfall magnitude. These results suggest that IC precipitation is primarily governed by storm dynamics, whereas OR precipitation is more sensitive to environmental forcing.

papers.title: The Growing Role of Evaporative Demand in Driving Record‐Breaking Droughts in the Amazon Basin
papers.snippet: Amazon droughts have historically been driven by precipitation deficits, but recent escalating drought events highlight a regime shift toward “hot droughts.” By decomposing historical drought drivers (1979–2024), we show that rising evaporative demand (represented by potential evapotranspiration, PET) now acts as a…
papers.abstract: Amazon droughts have historically been driven by precipitation deficits, but recent escalating drought events highlight a regime shift toward “hot droughts.” By decomposing historical drought drivers (1979–2024), we show that rising evaporative demand (represented by potential evapotranspiration, PET) now acts as a primary driver of drought intensification. While rainfall deficits remain the dominant contributor to the record‐breaking 2024 drought, escalating atmospheric thirst almost doubled its severity. Rising PET also expands the total drought footprint, disproportionately amplifying exceptional (D4) droughts and nearly tripling their affected area in 2024 compared to precipitation deficits alone. This PET increase is forced comparably by background warming and increased shortwave radiation; neutralizing either factor during 2024 reduces D4 drought coverage by 25%–33%. Linked to observationally confirmed declines in dry‐season cloud cover, these compounding thermodynamic and radiative feedbacks are driving a shift toward increasingly extreme hot droughts across the Amazon.

papers.title: Enhanced Retrieval of Raindrop Size Distribution by Integrating Disdrometer Observations and Atmospheric Variables With Machine Learning
papers.snippet: Accurate representation of raindrop size distribution (DSD) is crucial for understanding precipitation microphysics and improving quantitative precipitation forecasting.
papers.abstract: Accurate representation of raindrop size distribution (DSD) is crucial for understanding precipitation microphysics and improving quantitative precipitation forecasting. Conventional methods in numerical models often prescribe the DSD shape parameter as a constant or derive it from empirical relationships based solely on disdrometer observations, limiting their ability to capture DSD variability driven by dynamic, thermodynamic, and microphysical processes. This study develops a machine learning (ML) framework integrating disdrometer observations with environmental atmospheric variables to retrieve DSD parameters. Trained on data from 11 stations in Shanghai during 2019–2021, three ML models outperform conventional methods, effectively reducing biases and capturing observed DSD variability. They remain robust in independent heavy‐rainfall and tropical cyclone validations during 2022–2025, providing reliable DSD and rain rate estimates. Feature analysis and ablation experiments further underscore the critical role of environmental factors in improving retrieval accuracy, offering a data‐driven pathway to improve DSD parameterizations in numerical models.

Improved seasonal hydrological forecasting for Great Britain
papers.snippet: Great Britain's variable maritime climate has until relatively recently limited the utility of seasonal hydrological forecasts. The latest generations of seasonal atmospheric forecasting systems have created new opportunities to improve flow forecasting across Great Britain, such as for the UK Hydrological Outlook.
papers.abstract: Great Britain's variable maritime climate has until relatively recently limited the utility of seasonal hydrological forecasts. The latest generations of seasonal atmospheric forecasting systems have created new opportunities to improve flow forecasting across Great Britain, such as for the UK Hydrological Outlook. Here, we combine newly-developed high-resolution rainfall forecasts derived from historical weather analogues (HWA) conditioned on large-scale circulation patterns with a monthly-resolution national-scale hydrological model to produce seasonal and monthly forecasts. This forecasting scheme is evaluated using hindcasts from 1993–2017. We show that the skill of the rainfall forecasts is comparable to that achieved at coarser resolutions by other models. However, increasing the spatial resolution has degraded some of the skill found by previous authors producing HWA forecasts at lower resolutions. The river flow forecasts perform better than rainfall, with much of the improvement attributable to the skill provided by hydrological initial conditions. Both rainfall and river flow forecasts are most skilful in winter and perform adequately in spring and autumn. We show that in responsive catchments, primarily found in the northwest, rainfall forecasts contribute most of the skill in the river flow predictions but are much less important in regions with long hydrological memory. We thus indicate where flow forecasts would benefit most from improved rainfall forecasts or from better hydrological modelling.
